speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to press the Government on a matter of grave concern to a number of mentally and physically handicapped people in the Peace country, not to mention their families and friends who are concerned with their well-being.
These people with special needs have developed a feeling of pride, accomplishment, and skill, by being a part of the vocational training centre project. The project receives crucial federal funding. This on the job training project provided both trainees and the general public with a valuable learning opportunity.
This project is now about to come to an end as a result of the termination of the federal funding. The trainees will suffer. Roger Jackson, and the board of directors of the sponsoring association will see their dreams falter, and the friends and families of the trainees will lose hope for their loved ones. No comparable service is available in this northern community.
As well, Mr. Speaker, the Government will suffer because these trainees may well end up drawing unemployment insurance and social assistance, without training. This is how the Government will suffer because it will be spending without gain.
Surely the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts), who could find $140 million to provide jobs in Liberal ridings, can find a mere $200,000 in comparison, to help these people with special needs.

subsubtopic: IMAGE PROJECTED THROUGH DECLARATIONS BY CERTAIN SPOKESPERSONS FOR QUEBEC GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today, we read in La Presse and other newspapers that once again, representatives abroad of the Government of Quebec have been making statements about certain situations, and I am thinking for instance of the statement made by Mrs. Beaudoin about the Pope, who according to her, was not very well informed about the moral situation in this country or rather, in the Province of Quebec. Yesterday, the Premier of Quebec said the matter was blown out of all proportion and that it was a tempest in a teapot.
I suppose it is not terribly important to the Premier of Quebec. However, as a citizen of Canada and Quebec, I think that our international image is certainly not being improved by the Quebec Government's actions. Remember what happened , when the Premier of Quebec went to France? He said that once our senior citizens are dead, Quebec will vote for independence. Here again, he did not think what he said was terribly important. Another blunder was made when the Premier of Quebec went to Italy and said that the Italian President had expressed his support for the cause of independence. However, the President of Italy, through his Ambassador here in Canada, sent a number of documents back to the Premier, including his passport for "Quebec 1984".
Mr. Speaker, according to the Government of Quebec there is no problem. However, I am very concerned about the image we are projecting abroad, because of the actions of a province like Quebec. It is a shame that the Quebec Government, elected according to our democratic rules, refuses to consider the real situation in Quebec and is trying to get its message across through all kinds of underhanded manoeuvring, which can only have an adverse affect on the status of Quebecers and Canadians in general outside the country.

Mr. Speaker, last week the Minister of State for Social Development made a speech on behalf of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) to the Fisheries Council of Canada in which he spelled out the approach the Government will take to restructure the Pacific Fishing industry.
The Minister laid out a series of measures which are guaranteed to cause an uproar among fishermen and their communities. He then went on to say:
We hope and expect to receive the same level of co-operation from the opposition Parties that they gave last year to the Atlantic restructuring legislation.
I want to tell the Minister and his colleagues, clearly and plainly, that if he intends to treat this legislation in the same underhanded and irresponsible way as the Atlantic legislation, holding it back until the last possible moment in order to limit debate, and if he persists in bringing in legislation designed to restructure the industry by wiping out the livelihood of a large portion of the Pacific fishing fleet, he should not expect too much co-operation from this Party.
I serve notice that we will accept nothing less than a full debate in this House, and that we will press for the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry to travel to the West Coast to discuss the effect the rumoured legislation will have on fishermen and their communities.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) what steps the Liberal Government was taking to prevent financial institutions from demanding that Canadian home owners waive their rights before granting a mortgage renewal. The Minister had no answer, but he went on to suggest that home owners seek out other institutions to obtain more favourable terms.
All Canadian home owners with a mortgage know that if they seek out another institution it will cost them legal fees, appraisal fees, survey fees, and other costs. For a renewal on a $50,000 mortgage it could be as much as $1,000, whereas for a renewal with the same institution it would be a minimal fee.
It is unfortunate that the Minister of Finance has no idea of the problems of ordinary Canadians, and has no intention of helping them. The Liberal Government is simply standing by while mortgage interest rates continue to climb.

May 2, 1984

Mr. Speaker, 77 cents and sinking! The Canadian dollar continues to plunge on world markets as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) stands idly by, twiddling his thumbs. How can we instill confidence in the Canadian economy? How can we encourage investment? Most important, how can we create new jobs when our currency flounders about like that of a Third World banana republic?
The only response of the Liberals to the declining dollar has been to increase interest rates, a move which can only worsen the already ridiculously high level of unemployment. Canadians must, for our own sakes, make the necessary fundamental changes to our political economy so that our currency remains sound, investment is enhanced, and employment increases. Since the Liberals are unprepared to make these changes, it is high time they were replaced by a Conservative Government which will do so.

subsubtopic: "ETHICAL CHOICES AND POLITICAL CHALLENGES"-DOCUMENT ISSUED BY CATHOLIC BISHOPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring to the attention of the House the importance of the statement made yesterday by Bishops de Roo and Proulx, representatives of the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops. The Bishops, following on the landmark document which they released 16 months ago, have released a new report entitled "Ethical Choices and Political Challenges". They have again had the moral courage and conviction to point out the major problems which face this country, and to challenge the present Government, especially those candidates running for leadership of the Liberal party, to face those challenges.
In their report they lay out the stark reality that our present economic growth is characterized by soaring corporate profits and an almost complete lack of new job creation. While profits for banks and multinational companies in Canada hit record levels, two million Canadians cannot find productive work. The Government lacks any effective control over the new technologies and the profit-motivated priorities of the private sector which created these problems, yet insists that the private sector will solve our problems.
When we see the distribution of benefits in our society becoming increasingly unjust, as we have seen over the past few years, we have to ask what are our values and priorities. The Bishops have asked the right questions, and they should be thanked. It is up to the leaders of our country to provide honest and serious answers.
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, my question was for the Minister of Agriculture or the Minister of Finance. In their absence I will direct it to the Acting Prime Minister.
How can anyone justify or accept the high interest rates which were recently announced by the Farm Credit Corporation? The Minister must know that interest rates have risen from 13 per cent to 14 per cent for a five-year loan, and to 15 per cent on a 20-year loan. At the same time a farmer can get a loan from a chartered bank as low as 13.5 per cent. A home owner in the City of Toronto can get a mortgage at 13.25 per cent. The rates charged by the Farm Credit Corporation are closely tied to the cost of borrowing for a similar term by the federal Government. I am sure the Hon. Member is aware of this. There is a close relationship between what we have to pay for the money we borrow for similar terms and the rate at which we lend that money to farmers through the Farm Credit Corporation. The best evidence that the Farm Credit Corporation is running its operations very carefully in that regard to benefit the farmers is, as the Hon. Member knows, that the Corporation is not making a lot of money on its operations. On the contrary.
Mr. Speaker, we would not expect the Farm Credit Corporation to make any money. We would expect it to break even.

Mr. Speaker, that program was set up at a time when interest rates reached and, in fact, went over 20 per cent. The Hon. Member knows that since then there has been a very significant decline in interest rates both in Canada and the United States. Obviously the program was abandoned when there was a significant decline in interest rates.

subsubtopic: HIGH INCOME EARNERS-INCREASE IN NUMBER NOT PAYING TAXES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance who was busy yesterday trying to defend our very unfair personal income tax system. He made two points; first, that the loopholes used by the rich are available to everyone, and, second, that the system is fair. The Minister should try to explain to the ordinary worker or pensioner, or virtually anyone in the reasonable income category, where they are going to get the money to use those loopholes. He knows it is unfair.
My question really concerns the change in the system as it has developed in recent years. It relates to the fact that, between 1970 and 1981, those individuals earning over $100,000 and paying no tax increased in numbers from three to 1,500, and the number of those earning over $200,000 and paying no tax virtually doubled between 1980 and 1981.
Will the Minister acknowledge to the House that the reason we are seeing more and more rich individuals in Canada in a position where they are not paying their fair share is because the Government has introduced new tax loopholes for their benefit?

subsubtopic: HIGH INCOME EARNERS-INCREASE IN NUMBER NOT PAYING TAXES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would be typical of the New Democratic Party to qualify any incentive, complaining of the tax system, as a loophole. If the Hon. Member would look at the Income Tax Act he would see that there are a number of tax incentives which have been provided in order to encourage investment and stimulate the economy. Some of these incentives have to do with research and development, which is very important in creating jobs. Some have to do with capital investment or investment in equity, which this country needs. These incentives have been provided for all Canadians in order to encourage them to invest in the Canadian economy, thus stimulating economic growth.
I indicated something yesterday to the Hon. Member, and I will repeat it to him again today, taking a very simple example. You may have $100,000 of income this year but if, through your activities, the risks you have taken, you lost $150,000 last year, you are entitled to claim your loss last year against your income this year.

You may find yourself indeed with high income one year and no tax to pay, but it will be because you have incurred losses in order to help stimulate the economy and create jobs. He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-7 would enact the amendments to the Customs Tariff set out in the notice of ways and means motion tabled as part of last April's Budget.
Before noting a few details of the Bill, I should like to summarize the tariff amendments. First, improvements are being made in the rates of duty and other provisions of the general preferential tariff for developing countries. Second, we are increasing the limits on the value of goods that Canadians returning from abroad can bring home free of duty and tax. Third, duties on certain machinery parts are being increased. Finally, there are a number of miscellaneous changes affecting the dutiable status of a limited number of products.
The first group of tariff amendments which I should like to bring to the attention of the House relates to the general preferential tariff or what over a period of years has become known as the GPT. Hon. Members may recall that, as part of the 1981 Budget, there were a number of improvements made in the GPT, including new or lower rates on a broad range of products from developing countries. These rates had been recommended by the Tariff Board in response to a request from the Minister of Finance for a report on the impact on Canadian production of including new products under the GPT and of reducing to "free" the existing rates on other products.
The amendments in the Bill now before the House implement most of the recommendations made by the Tariff Board. That report was tabled in the House in May, 1982. Anyone interested can see the details in that report, on which interested parties were invited to comment. The comments received were carefully reviewed. While a few departures from the board's proposals have been made as a result, most of the board's recommendations are being adopted.
The amendments now before us provide for new or lower GPT rates, mainly free rates, on a wide range of products. The specific tariff amendments are set out in Schedule I to the Bill. The new lower rates would apply to qualifying imports, which in 1982 were valued at $11 million.
There are other amendments to the general preferential tariff included in this Bill which were not within the scope of the Tariff Board's study. The most noteworthy is the continuation of the general preferential scheme itself for another ten years to June 30, 1994.
Like Canada, most industrialized countries originally implemented their preferential tariff schemes for specified periods during which the impact of the preferences could be monitored and the need for their continuation determined. Those countries have also extended, or announced their intention to extend, their schemes. Canada's decision to extend the GPT rate was announced in May, 1982 by the Canadian delegation to a meeting of the Special Committee on preferences of the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development.
Provision has also been made in the Bill for a liberalization of the so-called "rules of origin" under the GPT. The purpose of these rules of origin is to ensure that only bona fide developing countries received the benefits of the general preferential
Customs Tariff
tariff. Goods substantially manufactured in industrialized nations which are shipped through GPT beneficiaries or have had only minor processing done on them in beneficiary countries are excluded from entry under the general preferential tariff by rules of origin. The rules are being amended so that value added in any GPT country will count toward the 60 per cent GPT content that products must have to be allowed entry at GPT rates.
Previously, the content requirement could be met only in the country from which the goods were being exported to Canada. This new measure was also announced by the Canadian delegation at the UNCTAD meeting I mentioned a moment ago and is in line with action taken by other industrialized countries.
Another change in the general preferential tariff is a new provision to give the Governor in Council authority to waive the requirement that goods must be shipped directly to Canada from GPT countries in order to qualify for GPT rates. This provision, which is similar to ones already in place for the British preferential and most-favoured-nation tariffs, will provide the authority needed for a flexible and speedy response to meet particular problems which arise from time to time with respect to shipments from developing countries. I might add that the Bill also includes a number of purely technical amendments to the GPT.
I should now like to turn to tourist exemptions. Prior to the April, 1983 Budget, the Department of Finance received many representations from individuals and several Members of this House asking that the value limitations on duty and tax-free exemptions for Canadians returning with purchases made abroad be increased. It was decided to meet those requests because the limits had not been increased since 1974. Their real value had been substantially eroded by inflation. The increases in the exemptions will also speed up customs clearance procedure, making it more convenient for travellers at our airports and other entry ports and reducing costs of administration.
The following are the specific changes in tourist exemptions. The quarterly exemption, available once in each calendar quarter after an absence of not less than 48 hours, is being increased from $50 to $100. The annual exemption, available once a year, after an absence of not less than seven days, is being increased from $150 to $300. The value of goods that can be brought back tax and duty-free under the "casual" exemption, which does not provide for a frequency limitation, is being doubled from $10 to $20. The minimum absence requirement under that casual exemption is being reduced from 48 to 24 hours.
In addition, the value of goods that can be entered under the tourist item which provides for a "flat" duty and tax rate is being increased from $150 to $300. The flat rate is being reduced from 25 percent to 20 per cent to take account of the lower duty rates applying as a result of the Tokyo round of GATT negotiations. There are also a number of purely technical changes in the tourist exemptions. All of these changes should make compliance with them less onerous for the travel-

May 2, 1984
Customs Tariff
ling public and should reduce government cost in administering these provisions.
The exemption increases included in this Bill are reasonable and respond to the representations and needs of the travelling public without having any adverse impact on Canadian business or on our balance of payments situation.
1 said something about the changes in the Bill respecting the general preferential tariff and the new provisions regarding tourist exemptions. I now want to turn to the tariff increases provided for in this Bill. Schedule III to this Bill contains amendments to certain machinery tariff items. While some of these amendments have the effect of lowering rates of duty, there are increases on feed pellet mill dies and rolls and on certain bulldozer parts.
Let me first say that the general policy of the Government is to work toward freer international trade and not to propose tariff increases, particularly in cases where existing rates are bound under international agreements such as the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, or GATT as it is commonly called.
Having said that, one might ask why we are proposing in this Bill to increase tariffs, even if the increases affect only a few specialized products. The answer is simply that these exceptions to the general rule are being made in the interest of equity.
During the Tokyo round of multilateral trade negotiations, it was decided to bind at "free" the rates of duty on a wide range of machinery and machine parts which had been entering Canada on a duty-free basis under the duty remission provisions of the machinery program on the grounds that they were unavailable from Canadian production. Some of the products covered by this agreement were dies and rolls used in feed pellet mills and a number of bulldozer parts.
Unfortunately, at that time Canadian officials were unaware that these particular articles were about to be made in Canada and that the Canadian manufacturers were counting on the fact that under the machinery program, a tariff could be applied to imports when production commenced. Accordingly, we have a situation where tariff protection considered necessary to the viability of Canadian manufacturing had been removed. In view of this, it was concluded that the appropriate duties on the feed pellet mill dies and rolls and bulldozer parts should be reinstated. Before these few tariff increases can come into effect, Mr. Speaker, they must be negotiated with our trading partners. These negotiations are now in progress. Accordingly, the Bill provides that the increases are to come into effect on a date to be proclaimed by the Governor in Council.
As I have mentioned, not all of the amendments in Schedule III provide for tariff increases. Provision is made for reduced rates on crawler loaders and crawler pipelayers and parts. These decreases together with the higher rates on the bulldozer parts essentially represent a package of tariff amendments
designed to standardize and simplify the tariff treatment of all crawler machines and parts.
In addition, the fourth major section of the Bill includes a number of miscellaneous tariff changes. The other tariff amendments set out in Clauses 5, 7, 8 and 9 and in Schedule III of the Bill do not have the significance or impact of the amendments which I have already noted. Many of these miscellaneous tariff changes are of a technical nature and are designed to reflect anomalies or to overcome administrative problems. Others are of a more substantive character, such as the new tariff items to implement the Tariff Board's interim report covering firebrick and other refractory products. These new items simplify and modernize the treatment of those products, taking into account representations made subsequent to the tabling of the board's report.
A new item is being introduced to provide duty-free entry for church carillons of a certain character. This item has been requested by a number of Members of the House on behalf of churches in their constituencies. The tariff on mixing consoles and tape recorders used by professional sound recording studios is being removed to assist the Canadian recording industry in its efforts to remain competitive by employing the most modern recording equipment.
Tariff-free provisions are also being established for certain other products from developing countries, and these products are set forth in the Bill. These miscellaneous changes are in line with the Government's policy of keeping our tariff responsive, within the limits imposed by our international obligations, to changing economic and technical needs.
I hope that the House will agree that these tariff measures should be given speedy passage since they do provide significant benefit, both to the developing countries and to Canadian manufacturers, Canadian importers and Canadian private citizens.

Mr. Speaker, we were not intending to take up a great deal of time on this Bill but we took a look at the Bill again and are rather disturbed by some of the things it contains. I wish to bring to the attention of the House the nature of this particular piece of legislation.
In brief, the legislation extends the general preferential tariff, that would normally have expired on June 30 of this year, until June 30 of 1994, a 10-year period. Second, as the Minister has indicated, it makes provisions for Canadians returning as tourists by doubling the amount of the former duty-free allowance on goods brought into the country. Third, the Bill does make certain tariff changes.
I would like to deal with the matter piece by piece. First, I would like to direct your attention, Sir, to the various schedules in this Bill. As you are perhaps aware, Sir, the tariff system in Canada includes four general tariff structures. The first tariff structure is the British preferential tariff. The next tariff is the most favoured-nationl tariff. Then there is a tariff called the general tariff, and finally a tariff called the general preferential tariff. All that sounds wonderful until one begins
May 2, 1984

to understand that all the countries in the world fall either under the British preferential tariff, the most favoured-nation tariff or the general preferential tariff, except for one country. There is one country in the world which we in this nation apparently hate, disdain, distrust and have no use for at all. That country, which must pay higher duties than any other country in the world on its imports into Canada, is the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.
Indeed, when looking at the Bill, one would find, for example, that if Saudi Arabia were to import vinegar into Canada, it would have to pay a 25 per cent tariff. However, the general preferential tariff on vinegar is free and the British preferential tariff on vinegar is 10 per cent. I do not know who is bringing vinegar into the country but if, for example, Saudi Arabia wished to import cigar boxes into Canada, it would have to pay a 35 per cent tariff. However, the general preferential tariff is free and the British preferential tariff is 11.3 per cent.
The Bill goes on. We all know the propensity of the Saudis to produce liquor. They are well covered by this tariff because the tariff on liquor from Saudi Arabia is dramatically higher than the tariff on liquor from any other country. I am thumbing through the Bill, Sir, so that I may tell you specifically what the amount of that tariff is. It is clear that the Saudis certainly would not be able to develop much of a market in Canada for their booze, if they should ever decide to produce booze, under the terms of this Bill. On bottled spirits like brandy, the Saudis would have to pay a $6 tariff, while the British preferential tariff is 75 cents. That is rather rough on the Saudis.
I believe that it is a bit ridiculous that the Government should produce a Bill which includes something called a general tariff when only one country in the world is subject to that tariff.
The Minister has come forward in the House and said that this is a great Bill. However, I would think that, when reviewing this piece of legislation, somewhere along the line we should simplify it. I believe that somewhere along the line, we should get rid of all this useless printing. I do not know, Sir, how much is imported into Canada from Saudi Arabia and I do not know why we should hit the Saudis with all these extra tariff charges that we do not charge any other country in the world, but that is what we do. I ask you, Sir, why should we deal with a Bill which contains schedules such as those in the Bill before us without giving it some deep consideration?
Beyond the points which I have already mentioned, Sir, we run into another series of tariff charts. In the course of preparing my comments on this Bill, I felt it was important to obtain a list of countries and their corresponding tariff arrangements from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). A great many countries fall not only under the most favoured-nation status but under the general preferential status and indeed the British preferential status as well. The usual arrangement is to use the lowest tariff. Why would a country not have only one tariff arrangement with Canada? Why would an importer have to find out which under the particular
Customs Tariff
circumstances would be the lowest tariff applicable to his country?
It is even more strange, Sir, to learn of some of the countries which fall under the most favoured-nation status. We have had difficulties with some countries in the world. We have had difficulties with the philosophy and the activities of the U.S.S.R., for example, but that country is considered to be a most favoured-nation. Hungary is a most favoured nation. Czechoslovakia is a most favoured nation. But poor old Romania is not only a most favoured nation, but it is entitled to a general preferential tariff because it is underprivileged. It has not only a rotten communist government, but it is most favoured. On top of that, it is entitled to general preferential treatment.
When one analyses this whole course of events, one begins to wonder under what circumstances and under what arrangements certain specific nations should have certain specific treatment from the Government. When we are discussing a Bill that affects the tariffs we are going to charge people bringing goods into the country, surely we should pay some attention to where we are going as a nation in terms of foreign trade. What kind of objectives have we got in terms of developing Canada and Canada's trade with the rest of the world? What kind of foreign aid stance should we take? If everyone is a somebody, then no one is an anybody. That is what we have here.
We pretend to assist certain countries of the world with trade preferences by giving them the benefit of the general preferential tariff, but the fact is that we give that general preferential tariff to virtually every country of the world. There is no real, specific benefit to those countries that perhaps we are trying as a nation to help.
Second, it is apparent, when one analyses the chart of the tariffs available, that some countries whose trading activities are such as to damage Canadian industry and who organize their affairs in such a way as to prevent Canadians from having reasonable access to their home markets, are given by this Government general preferential tariff treatment when they bring their goods into Canada. We are the proverbial good boy scouts. We take a kneeing every time we deal with them, yet we allow them to bring their goods into our country in many cases virtually, duty-free.
I specifically draw to the attention of the House the problems we have had in the aircraft industry. This House has been beset with problems concerning de Havilland. One of the problems de Havilland has is the unfair competition that it is experiencing from an aircraft corporation owned, operated and run by the Brazilian Government. Yet Canada gives to Brazil general preferential tariff rating on all of its imports into Canada. We do so even though Brazil will not allow us anything like that type of preference when we are selling our goods to Brazil, even though the Brazilians operate in the aircraft field and in the financing of aircraft in such a fashion

May 2, 1984
Customs Tariff
as to damage seriously and mortally our exports of aircraft from de Havilland into the South American market.
It is absolutely ridiculous that we should continue to give certain countries general preferential tariff benefits when their trading stance and the way they operate in the world is to do damage to Canadians and to Canadian business. I think it is important that the Government be prepared to go over the various countries with the House and declare and explain why this Government is prepared to give various countries the general preferential tariff rate it is obviously, by this Bill, intending to extend. There has to be a rethinking as to who should get trade advantages with Canada.
I think Canada has an obligation to help certain of the less fortunate people in the world. We have to help them help themselves, because I think we owe that to the world as good citizens. But surely as good citizens of the world we should not dilute that assistance by giving it willy-nilly to everyone, willy-nilly to those who really do not justify that assistance. For example. South Korea was certainly an underdeveloped country at one time, but now it has virtually taken the world over in terms of shipbuilding and in terms of steel. Indeed, we have had to put anti-dumping charges against steel imports coming from that country. There comes a point when an underdeveloped country ceases to be entitled to privileges beyond what is reasonable. That is particularly so when the trade arrangements we have with those countries are prejudicial to Canada and when those countries operate in such a fashion as to use Canada as a dumping ground for their products to the detriment of Canadian industry and Canadian jobs.
When we deal with a Bill of this nature, the Government has an obligation to talk not only about housekeeping changes in tariff structures, but it has an obligation to say how this particular piece of legislation improves opportunities for Canadians, improves job opportunities for Canadians, and improves business opportunities for Canadians. If one is looking at it from an aid point of view, it helps foreign aid opportunities to justify Canada's place in making this a better world. This Bill does not do anything of that nature. It just covers the waterfront and carries on with the same old scheme that has lost all sense of validity when we give preferences to everyone. We have no sense of a constant tariff provision. There is no rationale in our tariff rates. The Minister was not prepared in his explanation to defend the rationale behind the tariff-setting system.
Tariffs are something we use-perhaps they are not as valid today as they were at one time-as an inducement to other countries to allow them, force them, or encourage them to give Canadians an opportunity to trade in their countries. When a country sells goods to us at no tariff or at a very much reduced tariff, we expect that country to give to our exporters, manufacturers, and vendors of goods opportunities in its market. Trade is a two-way street.
Over two million Canadians depend on foreign trade for their livelihood. Under this Government our share of world trade since 1968 has slipped from 5.8 per cent to 3.7 per cent.
If we were able to increase our share of world trade by 1 per cent today, we could increase the number of jobs held by Canadians by very close to 600,000. Yet, does this Bill do anything toward that aim or objective? Not on your life. There are in it just a few housekeeping amendments to allow Canadians to come in with $300 worth of goods when they could have brought in only $ 150 before. It does not even put any imagination into the subject.
We have an obligation when we are considering a Bill of this nature to ask the Government where we are going in foreign trade. Where does this Bill, in terms of tariff protection for Canadian industry and the change in that protection, help Canadian industry or, in the converse, help Canadians get into foreign markets? There is precious little in this Bill, Sir, which in any way helps.
The Minister mentioned bulldozer parts. He said he was increasing the tariff on bulldozer parts. Well, that is what the Bill is all about. The Bill also, I am told, Sir, if I have it correctly, reduces the tariff on certain mynah birds, which are members of the starling family and which have traditionally been allowed into the country. The Bill is to amend the Act to exempt the Chinese Talking mynah bird and the Hill mynah bird.
It is like a "mynah" bill.

My friend says it is a "mynah" bill.
Somewhere along the line there has to be some better explanation as to why we should be changing the tariffs of Canada other than to deal with the problem of mynah birds. There is no provision in this Bill whereby the Government can make specific exemptions to specific countries on tariffs. A country falls within one of four categories. Most countries get some kind of preference, all except the Saudis, I would say. However, surely to goodness if we are going to improve our trade position, or if we are to be able to extend a helping hand to a specific foreign country which needs that help, there should be some specific direction, some specific look at each country's position and how that country should be treated vis-a-vis Canada. This Bill does not do that.
Let me speak for a moment about the British preferential tariff. You may recall, Sir, that in the early 1930s, the Government of the late R. B. Bennett created, as a result of the Commonwealth Conference, the British preferential tariff. That was the first preferential tariff that we ever had in this country. It was followed later by a most-favoured nation type arrangement. The British preferential tariff was a special arrangement which went a long way to holding the Commonwealth together and giving Canada significant trading opportunities. As a result, a number of subsidiaries of Canadian companies were created around the world. I specifically think of the Canadian subsidiaries of the Ford Motorcar Company, for example, in what is now Zimbabwe. That subsidiary was created because it was an agency in South Africa where Canadian Ford automobile parts and components were sent
May 2, 1984

and converted into automobiles there, and that was of benefit to Canada. The British preferential tariff has pretty well disappeared as an advantage now because, indeed, aside from certain trade arrangements with Australia and New Zealand, the British preferential tariff is not as good as the general preferential tariff accorded to most Commonwealth countries. As far as most Commonwealth countries are concerned, they carry on under the general preferential tariff.
It would seem to me, Sir, that in proceeding with this Bill, the Government should do some rethinking. The Government should say that, in a sense, the British preferential tariff system has served its purpose and that it should be set aside, removed. The countries in the British Commonwealth which qualify for the British preferential tariff as well as the general preferential tariff should perhaps benefit from the general preferential tariff, and other countries should have the regular tariff. I believe we could probably organize in such a way as to get along with one or two tariffs: first, a tariff structure for all countries in the world and, second, a tariff structure for those specific underdeveloped countries where an easy access to the Canadian market would help. I feel we no longer need four tariff structures. Obviously, the general tariff structure does not mean anything. Only the Saudis pay that. The British preferential tariff system really means very little. Why could we not, then, handle the whole matter with two structures? That would simplify things dramatically. We could have one structure which was a regular tariff and one structure which gave to underdeveloped, less developed, nations a special privilege or preference in Canada.
In doing this, it would be my submission that we should analyse carefully those countries to which we want to give special privilege. It should be countries which are growing, countries we can help. It should not be every country in the world, or every underdeveloped country in the world, but only certain undeveloped countries which should be given virtually tariff-free access to Canada. The rest of the world should pay the same tariff. We should not discriminate. That does not mean that, in not discriminating, we cannot make separate arrangements with countries which are not included for specific items of trade. That would be a sectoral approach to what are perhaps special bilateral trade arrangements on special goods from special countries.
It would seem to me that in the interests of the country we should move ahead. This Bill should be redrawn and simplified, and if we make tariff item changes, we should make them after rethinking them. This, Sir, is what I recommend to the House.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Is the House ready for the question?
The Hon. Member for Edmonton South (Mr. Roche).

Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to detain the House unduly, but I want to make a few comments on the trade liberalization aspects of the Bill before us. First of all, the changes made in extending the preferential tariff treatment which are listed are not an altruistic measure
Customs Tariff
taken by Canada. Indeed, they are in harmony with the move today in the world to recognize that each country benefits according to the way in which it facilitates its trade with other nations. If we are going to be able to sell Canadian goods to those expanding, developing country markets where huge population increases are happening, we have to enable those countries to reach into Canada. Therefore, I support this Bill.
However, I believe that my colleague, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) has made an extremely important point in calling to our attention the failure of the Bill-and even the Minister's own speech-to indicate clearly enough that when certain countries increase their ability to perform-as we say, they graduate-they would no longer receive preferential treatment.
I was glad to see that the Bill before us follows, or at least it certainly takes note of, one of the principal recommendations made to the House by the parliamentary Committee on North-South Relations which reported to the House about two years ago. In the section on trade we recommended that the general preferential tariff be extended to include all manufactured goods of the world's poorest countries, and that graduation criteria be established to identify those countries no longer in need of preferential treatment. As both myself and my colleague from Mississauga South pointed out, Mr. Speaker, the Government had failed in this Bill to indicate clearly that the extensions of the general preferential tariff are supposed to be aimed at those least developed countries. That is a very important principle which ought to be followed.
In a statement the Minister said he wanted the developing countries to receive the benefits of the preferential tariff, but he did not specify or make clear that as Canada increases or liberalizes its trade benefits, we have in mind those countries which truly need access to our markets if they are going to be able to develop some self-reliance and become full partners in the trading system of the world. We have to consider why the Minister's speech, indeed the Bill, are inadequate responses to the points raised by my colleague and by myself.
The answer, Mr. Speaker, is that Canada today does not have a strategy for international development. We had a strategy from 1975 to 1980, some of which was implemented, some not. But at least it was a clear course of direction, covering trade matters, international financial institutions and development assistance. There was a course of action that the Canadian people and this House could see clearly. We are now in the fourth year of the subsequent decade and there is still no strategy for the 1980s. I would certainly like to have the Minister's view on why the Government does not have a full strategy for international development and Canada's role therein. If that were the case, it would be clear for everyone to see why these partial measures are being taken. It would also be clear whether we are in fact aiming this Bill at the least developed and most heavily populated countries of the world, or whether we are being less discriminating in our trade moves.

May 2, 1984
Customs Tariff
Before I leave the subject of the North-South committee's recommendations, I want to draw to the attention of the House that, although the Government has accepted our recommendation concerning the general preferential tariff extension to some extent, it has yet to respond to what we considered at that time, based on a very extensive analysis of trade conditions, that there be a major public inquiry on the question of adjustment measures. We know that if we are to allow greater entry to the products of developing nations, that is going to cause dislocation in the Canadian economy. I do not know any politician in his right mind who would advocate measures which will throw his own people out of work. The most famous example of this is, of course, the textile industry. It is well known that the Canadian textile industry is shored up by subsidies and that textiles can be produced at a much lower cost in many other countries, as indeed they are. Yet it would be an irresponsible measure for any of us to recommend holus-bolus that we close down the Canadian textile industry in an effort to provide more jobs in the developing world. Having said that, it is clear as we move into the post-technological society-whatever this new society of computership and high technology is going to be called-that we have to set a course, examine our industrial strengths and set into motion a process of conversion of those industries no longer competitive in the global economy.
In a very strong recommendation the North-South committee suggested that the Government immediately launch a major public inquiry of the industrial sectors which are likely to be at long-term competitive disadvantage in relation to developing countries, with a view to adopting effective adjustment measures. In light of that, I fail to recognize why the Government has just turned its back. The Government responded that it agreed with the thrust of our report, but I am calling the attention of the House to this fundamental need for a public inquiry into the adjustment measures which are going to be required if Canada is going to be able to modernize its productive capacity so that it harmonizes with the global demand for an increase in world trade generally. My colleague has already stated that Canada's share of world trade has slipped from 5.8 per cent to 3.7 per cent. Surely that is sufficient evidence to impel us to take measures to increase our share. Surely that is the motivation for taking those steps which will increase the capacity of the growing population of the developing world to buy from us. Trade is a two-way street, Mr. Speaker.
Changes are called for, for example, in the international development strategy for the 1980s, which was adopted by consensus at the United Nations in 1980. I believe the measures set out in the international development strategy should be adopted by Canada as a proponent nation, recognizing the truth today in the North-South dialogue that the global economy is so interdependently structured that when the North goes into recession, as we have done, we cannot come out of it until the South is given an opportunity for its own expansion. We cannot live by ourselves. It is not simply a
question of altruism to put forth that viewpoint; it is a question of economic survival.
The international development strategy was conceived and developed along those lines. The world being in an economic crisis today is a further reason for Canada to project its own international development strategy for the remaining decade of the 1980s.
I have just returned from Peru, which is a country that has a major aid program from the Canadian Government. If one wants to see all the effects of the complex web of relationships today in one location, even a small location like Peru, that is the place to see it. We see the effects of the debt crisis. The debt crisis in many countries is caused by the bottom falling out of their commodity export markets while they have to pay more for the importation of manufactured goods from industrialized countries. The debt crisis is caused by the gap widening between their exports earnings and the cost of imports. This debt crisis, which is now of staggering dimension, is affecting countries all over the world, but it is particularly noticeable in Latin American countries, which perhaps had too easy an access to the banking institutions of the 1970s which wanted to lend them money under the concept of a never ending expanding world economy.
Peru is an example of how the debt crisis has meant a larger cutback in development programs for its own people. There are people in developing countries today who are farther behind in achieving their own self-reliance than they were a few years ago, even with all the development assistance that is still taking place. I am quite sure that the Minister recognizes as well as I do the reality of what I am saying. It gives more truth to my earlier comment that we must be able to put together a package that includes the items of international development assistance, preferential trade relationships, and the development of indigenous energy supplies, both renewable and nonrenewable. This package must include the enlargement of the international financial institutions, particularly the facilities within the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. We must develop an entire enlarged package that can be sustained by the sufficiency of world liquidity, which exists today, in order that Canadians and the Canadian Government have a meaningful relationship with the expanding populations of the world with whom we have an interdependent relationship.
Those are some of the general comments that I felt impelled to make because of what I regard to be a piecemeal legislation that approaches a very serious and deep problem from a rather narrow base. I believe that there is an opportunity for Canada to play a constructive role in the enlargement of the world economy. We cannot do this alone since we are too small and have too many problems in our own country. However, it is to our own advantage to play a greater role in the push for global economic negotiations as a means of implementing the international development strategy for the 1980s. It is in our interest to do this.

May 2, 1984
I say to the Minister very frankly that I believe there is a lack of impetus and momentum in the Government today in the development of our relations.
I believe Canada should take an approach that would incorporate Bill C-7 into a larger framework which would have a much more meaningful impact on the international community and would indeed benefit the Canadian people and result in the creation of more jobs in our society. Such an approach would reflect a greater concern about the staggering effects of the rising debt burden on developing countries, the monetary policies of industrialized countries and the trade barriers that still exist, despite some of the piecemeal benefits in the present legislation. We have yet to recognize that the economic recovery of industrialized countries depends on the ability of growing markets in other parts of the world, particularly in the developing countries, to buy.
When we recognize that millions will continue to face starvation if we do not make the necessary structural improvements in the world institutions, it becomes a two-pronged motivation for greater action. There is a political and economic imperative that challenges us as politicians to do this. There is a human imperative that challenges us as human beings to do this. 1 have just given the example of my most recent examination of this subject in Peru. As human beings we should recognize that the extended suffering of millions upon millions of people is not a proper basis for any kind of society to call itself advanced in a world of technology that is able to produce sufficiently to feed and house every member of the human community.
We have taken some satisfaction from the fact that all of us are agreed as political Parties that Canada must reach .7 per cent of Gross National Product in international development assistance by 1990. 1 think that is a recognition of a sense of concern that is present in the House. Certainly, it is present in the country. When all is said and done, despite different approaches which people take on economic subjects, we want to do the right thing within our capacity to do it. I believe that reaching .7 per cent by 1990 would be, in my view, a minimal requirement.
The point I want to make here and on which this bill touches is that development aid is only a fraction of what needs to be done to build the economies of the South. It is not development assistance that will build the economies. It is, I would even say, of marginal benefit to developing countries. It is the enlargement of their capacity to become self-reliant; it is the enlargement of their capacity to plug into world trade. This Bill begins to approach that.
However, there are a number of steps that could be taken, and I believe this Bill could be viewed as a foundation. There are a number of steps that need to be taken if Canada is to be fully involved in contributing to the expansion of the world economy.
I think that Canada through the United Nations' system, which is intimately involved in all the intricacies of the subject,
Customs Tariff
should work to expand the resources and quotas of the International Monetary Fund so that that fund itself could provide, along with the facilities of the World Bank, access to the least developed. We are seeing now the effects of the stringent conditionality of the IMF in many countries that are turning to it for assistance because of the debt crisis. We saw only last week the results of such stringent measures in Dominica where there were riots as a result of controls being put on the local economy with deleterious political effects in the country. We are going to have more of that if ways are not found to increase the capacity of the international financial institutions to respond to today's need. That is going to require, I think, more of a sense of commitment that perhaps we hoped we were going to see as the North-South Summit was held in Cancun in the fall of 1981, which once more failed to deliver the goods.
I think that Canada must take an active part in efforts to initiate a process of basic reform of world trade and financial arrangements. This reform will take the nature, in the main, of an enlargement of the facilities within the institutions. It should take a much more vigorous look at the effects of protectionism, and we should commit ourselves to contributing actively to negotiations within GATT and preparatory discussions regarding a new trade round.
I think the GATT results of its most recent trade round were certainly of some benefit, but marginal compared to the need. And, similarly, with more leadership in the GATT system in an effort to develop further the integration of developing nations into GATT, we have to pay much more attention to what UNCTAD is attempting to do in enlarging the trade capacities of developing countries.
I have to say with some real regret that the most recent UNCTAD conference in Belgrade, which I think was held about a year ago-I do not know whether you can call any conference a failure; it is not a failure if people come out of it still talking to each other,-certainly did not accomplish anything toward the enlargement of the trade capacity of developing nations, and again I say that the enlargement of that trade capacity is in the interests of the whole North-South dialogue. I believe a re-examination is needed in terms of a new GATT round and a much more serious effort made to respond to the message of UNCTAD in acting against protectionist trade barriers.
Finally, we need to develop a new strategy of international development co-operation, as I have said, that would respond to and harmonize with the United Nations international development strategy for the 1980s. 1 do not think that much in this way can be done realistically until there is greater public awareness in our country and greater public education of the people on the complexities of the international monetary and trading system of the world today.
When we look at relations with developing countries, the reality is that this subject goes so far beyond CIDA and so-called foreign aid or international development assistance, it goes so far beyond it, as I indicated a moment ago, as to render almost marginal those activities of an aid nature, when the real

May 2, 1984
Customs Tariff
need is to enlarge the productive capacity of the whole world in such a way that we increase our trading capacity one with another.
We have failed to keep pace in Canada. Not only have we lost our share of world trade in the life of this Government, not only have we declined from 5.8 per cent to 3.7 per cent of world trade, but we have not kept pace with the United States, Japan, and EEC in the enlargement of their trade with developing countries. Our trade balance on both sides, import and export, with developing nations is somewhere around 12 per cent, maybe 13 per cent. In the case of the United States, Japan and the EEC, it varies from, say, 20 per cent to the low 40s.
I have taken this moment to use the opportunity, which the minister provides us by bringing in what I call a piece-meal Bill, to remind the Government of its responsibilities and its obligations to take a much more sweeping approach through publishing a strategy, setting out a course of action to help Canadians understand the dimensions, and also to make the point that it is in our own interests to do these things.
I come from Edmonton South. I can tell you there are people today out of work in Edmonton South who were never out of work before in their lives. Why are they out of work today? Because of the recession and because of the cutbacks in the productive capacity of some of their own industries. I am leaving aside here the whole question of the deleterious impact of the National Energy Program on the economy of my own province and my own city. I feel pretty strongly about that, but I do not want to make a political attack on the Government in this speech because I really want to make an effort to have the Government listen and respond to this need for an enlargement of thinking in our approach to the construction of policy of a trading international financial institution and energy and commodity pricing of all those elements that are at the basis of the international economy today. The Government should hear how it would be in the interests of those people in Edmonton South who are out of work, were they able to witness and participate in a replugging of Canada into the industrial economic growth of industrialized countries, starting with ourselves.
There is a crisis in the world today. It is a crisis which has many dimensions. Bankers are replete with their own definitions of this crisis. It is a crisis of people in our country who are out of work as a result of the failure of the economy to expand. There is a crisis in developing countries where their debt is so horrendous that it results in a cutback in their own development programs. There is a cutback in the lives of people who are suffering as a result of the inability of the world economy to get going again.
I say to the Government that we now have a tremendous opportunity to use our ability to build an economy which can reach out to the expanding world in a way that lifts up Canadians and helps to make us a full participant as a vigorous and vibrant nation in a growing world economy,
leading to some economic stability and a sense of social justice for the world.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I should like to join in this debate for a few moments. Often when we are considering a Bill of which most in the House take little note, a Bill such as Bill C-7, it is wise to take a little more in-depth look at what we are talking about. For example, what is this Bill that the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. MacLaren) seemed to pass off so lightly in his opening remarks? He used the term once or twice that it was a kind of housekeeping Bill.
The main thrust of my remarks today will be that I believe the House of Commons is not acutely aware enough of what the export-import or general trade picture of Canada is all about. Tied in with that, of course, we must give more thought to the question of customs tariff. Are we indeed dealing with the rest of the world in the most prudent way?
Since I have been in the House of Commons, the Bill we are now considering amending has been amended 11 other times. For example, it was amended in 1973. It was amended three further times in the period from 1974 to 1975. In the period from 1976 to 1977, it was amended four times. In the 1977-78 session, it was amended again. Again it was amended in 1979-80. Finally, it was amended in the 1980-81-82 session.
If we attempt to identify what is the existing law, bearing in mind the Revised Statutes of Canada which are dated 1970, we find that this is one of the most confusing pieces of legislation on the statute books of Canada. Granted, we can go to the Canada Statute Citator and go through the various amendments. However, I am suggesting that because of the amendments and the basic complexity of the Bill, it is now almost impossible for the average Member of the House to come up with a meaningful position, for example, with respect to Clause 2 of Bill C-7. I refer to Clause 2 because it sounds so innocent. It simply reads:
Section 3.7 of the said Act is repealed and the following substituted therefor-
The net effect of that clause would be to have the expiry date for Sections 3.1 to 3.6 lengthened from 1984 to June 30, 1994. It is not until we go to the Citator that we see the true significance of that 10-year extension. Mr. Speaker, I know that you follow these statutes very closely; perhaps it is no news to you. However, I think it would be news to many people in Canada if I indicated what in fact is being covered by that rather innocent Clause 2 to which I have referred.
In fact, in the Canada Statute Citator there are literally pages of amendments to the 1970 Customs Tariff Act, as it appears in the Statutes of Canada, which are now being amended by Clause 2. I will not read into the record-because Hon. Members who are interested will do it-the two to three dozen subsections affected by what is being proposed in Clause 2. I am simply using it as an illustration of how casual Ministers of the Crown can become with regard to Bills which they are introducing.
May 2, 1984

To use the words the Minister dropped on us, he hoped that there would be speedy passage. Why did he hope that there would be speedy passage? It was probably because he does not know what the Bill means. Certainly he would not entertain questions. He would be most embarrassed if I asked him questions about any of those three dozen subsections to which I have referred and which will be affected by Clause 2 of Bill C-7. I will go further and suggest that the Minister has not even read those subsections, yet he recommended a speedy passage.
I should like to deal with Clause 3 of the Bill before us. Again it sounds innocent. It simply reads:
Section 11 of the said Act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
Then it continues:
The Governor in Council may, by order,
(a)	make such reductions of duties on goods imported into Canada from any
other country or countries as may be deemed reasonable by way of compensation for concessions granted by any such country or countries; and
(b)	extend any reduction made pursuant to paragraph (a) to any other
countries as may be required by Canada's international obligations.
It is subsection (b) which is really the amendment. However, I should like to point out that when one reads that subsection, one naturally asks, "What is the effect of including it?" Then one looks to the explanatory notes and sees that the section I have just read is the same as that in paragraph 3 of the Budget motions introduced with the Budget on December 7. In short, you are told nothing. All you are told is that on February 7 the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) tabled in the House a motion that had the same words as Clause 3 which now appears in the Bill with no further explanation. Most people would be interested in why the Minister felt it was necessary in December to move the motion. The Minister did not touch today on why we are now being asked to give speedy passage to this Bill, including Clause 3. I raise that because I did a little homework. I thought we should check into Subclause (b) to find the reason they have extended the first paragraph, which reads:
Extend any reduction made pursuant to paragraph (a) to any other countries as may be required by Canada's international obligations.
The bottom line is that they have added that subclause because they do not want to come back to this House. They want the ultimate in freedom. At the present time the Government is able to negotiate with countries under the present Section 2 of the Customs Tariff Act. As I indicated, it has the right to make compensation for concessions given by other countries.
Apparently because they have to make those changes in a spirit of bartering or negotiation, there are certain circumstances that may trigger the necessity also to include other countries. That is what they mean by "extend any reduction made pursuant to paragraph (a) to any other countries as may be required by Canada's international obligations". Does that wording have to be that wide? Is it really appropriate for this House of Commons, which represents the people of Canada, to
Customs Tariff
say, not to any designated Minister but to the Cabinet; "If you think it is necessary to make a change and extend that change to any other country as may be required by Canada's international obligations, you go ahead and do it and don't worry us about it"? That is what we are being asked to do.
Think of the implications, Mr. Speaker. What does the Government mean by "Canada's international obligation"? Is it talking about aid obligations? Is it something to do with the CIDA program, our obligations in NATO or our obligations to such international financial institutions as the World Bank? We do not know. We are being asked to give the Government the right, a blank cheque, to extend as it sees fit any reduction made pursuant to paragraph (a) to any other country as may be required by Canada's international obligations.
Not only do I raise the question of how complicated this Bill has become. Not only is it a question of all the amendments to which I am referring. We also have to realize that if the Government has its way with the Bill in its present form, it will take even more away from the House of Commons than we have had taken away over the last decade.
It is not time for us to consider that because of the complexities and the admitted difficulties of moving quickly, of making deals with international countries and partners that perhaps have to be finalized without undue delay, it is necessary to have a committee of this House meet on a constant basis to consider whatever those in Revenue Canada feel is needed in the line of either regulation or amendments to existing legislation?
If they feel they have a deal cooking with one or more countries that may, if entered into, require some type of change with other countries because of Canada's so-called international obligations, surely a committee of this House could be structured. In a preliminary way it could hear the problem and advise the respective caucuses as to whether it thinks the Government is right or wrong. I do not feel in an elected House of Commons that it is proper for this type of further delegation to be made. It is not appropriate for us to say: "Do not ask for whatever authority you need in specifics but ask in a blanket way and the more you shelter us from what you're doing, the better".
I do not want to fault Revenue Canada or, for that matter, the implications of the customs legislation generally, but the fact is that we have not done well under the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) with respect to trade with the developing world. My colleague from Edmonton highlighted some of the problems. If you review trade with the developing world, Mr. Speaker, you find that in the case of European countries about 30 per cent of their trade at the present time is with the developing world. In the case of Japan it is about 30 per cent. Of all the trade the Japanese are doing with every country of the world, about 30 per cent is with developing world countries. In the case of the United States it is 43 per cent. In the case of Canada it is 10 per cent.
We have to start asking what has gone wrong under the "emperor" who, when he became emperor in the country in 1968, said that he was going to explore a third alternative. He
May 2, 1984

Customs Tariff
was going to shift our trade away from the American orientation to what he called the third option. If you check the figures, Mr. Speaker, you see that in 1965 when the Prime Minister spoke about shifting the orientation that we then had with the United States, total trade with the United States as far as the Canadian side was concerned was about 65 per cent. When the emperor took over, 65 per cent of our trade was with the United States. Now that he is leaving us it is 73 per cent. We have 8 per cent more of our trade now with the Americans than when the emperor began his reign.
When this type of thing is happening, is it not time for us in the House of Commons to begin taking a better look at legislation such as Bill C-7 and to say: "We need more input to make sure that you fellows are not going to continue to make the mistakes that you have been making with respect to export-import trade and, in particular, with respect to the levers that you may have, such as customs legislation." I am suggesting that a committee of the House could meet constantly to take a better look at this Bill.
Second, I am suggesting that we should not, without due consideration, let more authority be taken from the House and given to the Cabinet of the day as is contemplated by Clause 3. In effect, Clause 3 would simply say to the Cabinet: "If you think some international obligation is affected by some deal that you have cooked up, go ahead and make the changes without reference to the House". Too much is at stake for us to consider that.
I only wish that I had a little more time to speak, Mr. Speaker, because I would like to deal with the question of raising the duty free amount of money that Canadians can spend in foreign lands. These exemptions are coming at a time when we are living with such a severe external imbalance. At a time when our dollar is now coming close to 77 cents, is it not strange that we are telling Canadians that they can go out of the country and buy twice as much as before because we do not want to keep them unduly limited by these exemptions? Surely the time has come for the House to begin taking a more serious look at the question of whether or not this is really in the best interests of all Canadians. We must bear in mind that this change has already been put in place. If this Bill is passed, it will have retroactive effect to April 20, 1983.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: There follows a ten-minute period for questions and comments. I would like to caution Hon. Members at this point that although the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) made reference to clauses in the Bill, discussion at second reading is on the principle of the Bill and questions or comments should not deal with specific clauses.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) a question. The Bill, an amendment to the Customs Tariff Act, contains a whole series of schedules which deal with the British preferential tariff, the most favoured-nation tariff, the general tariff and the general
preferential tariff. Is it the view of the Hon. Member that we need four separate tariffs, bearing in mind that the general tariff now applies only to Saudi Arabia? Is it his view that the Saudis should be penalized by being the only country in the world required to pay $6 a bottle for booze imported into Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I listened very carefully to the comments of the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) when he was making the case as to why the four schedules to which he has referred appear to be almost out of date or archaic. I think he has made a good point. If there is substantiation for his argument that Saudi Arabia is the only country that seems to have been isolated in this way, I find it to be a most strange turn of events.
In line with what I said earlier, I think it would be very helpful if not only the schedules in the Bill but the entire Bill itself was overhauled and streamlined with the hope that more people who are dealing with this type of legislation in a day-to-day sense can deal with it and understand what it means without hiring high-priced brokers and others who must intercede and who in many cases themselves do not even understand the effects of many of these clauses and schedules. My short answer to my hon. colleague would be that if, at committee for example, he is able to substantiate what he has said concerning the situation of Saudi Arabia, I believe it must be rectified and rectified quickly.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for York-Peel is our Party's external affairs critic and that position would obviously have a great deal of reference to trade. I was wondering if he had taken a look at the question of whether the British preferential tariff had any real value any longer and whether it would be possible to simplify the entire tariff structure by having one general tariff and a separate preferential tariff for under-developed nations with which we may want to deal on a special basis. I wonder if it is his view that we could perhaps get rid of the British preferential tariff, particularly bearing in mind that it really does not offer much in the way of preference to any nation and bearing in mind the fact that Great Britain and Ireland are now members of the European Community.

Again, Mr. Speaker, in reply to the question of my hon. colleague, I think this is an excellent example of how the statute is rather out of date in so many ways. The term "British preferential tariff' is a term which presumably came from the days of the British Empire and the British Commonwealth and is simply not in tune with today's terminology. I see no reason that there could not be a smoothing out and simplification of the terminology and schedules to which my hon. colleague has referred.
I have in front of me the Canada Statute Citator which is published every year by McGoldrick. It is very difficult to find this in the customs tariff section of that book but the book does set out exactly which countries are treated as British preferential tariff countries. If any Hon. Members are interested, I could tell them which countries are included under that tariff.
May 2, 1984

If any Hon. Members are curious as to whether or not Christmas Island, the Cocos Islands, Guyana, Lesotho, Ghana and India are included, I could give them the answer.
In answer to my colleague's question, I would say we do not need so many schedules. We do not need so many so-called preferential categories. Those categories could be simplified and I hope that when this Bill gets to committee one of the things which would be explored with the Minister and his officials is why this is not being proposed at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question of my colleague, the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens), which concerns an area of Ontario with which I think the Hon. Member is very familiar, the Lindsay area. There is a manufacturing plant there which manufactures inner tubes and some minor rubber products. That plant has been very adversely affected by the importation of products from South Korea and Taiwan.
I directed the officials of that plant to the Anti-Dumping Tribunal which ruled that there was not sufficient evidence to determine that dumping was occurring. A considerable number of jobs were lost at this plant which means a lot to the community. I think the officials of the plant were probably given the brush-off by the Anti-Dumping Tribunal and I have a deep concern over the number of people whose jobs will be affected.
I believe we see too much evidence of small plants trying to establish themselves, employing up to 50 people and then running into deep trouble because of foreign goods coming into the country at a much, much lower price. I would like to hear the views of the Hon. Member about situations like that.

Mr. Speaker, the point made by the Hon. Member illustrates why Members of the House should be taking a much deeper interest in the type of legislation that is now before us. I am suggesting that there could be a committee of this House before which the Minister and the officials of Revenue Canada could explain why they want to make these changes. That would be a good idea because it would help cover the very points raised by my colleague.
We all recall that the last round of tariff negotiations in Geneva was held in almost complete secrecy. We had negotiators there, but the rank and file manufacturer in Canada-the people who were going to be affected-had no direct input.
That is in complete contrast to the American approach. The Americans, first of all, went to their manufacturers, invited them to attend and hear what proposals were going to be raised in Europe, and asked for their comments and criticisms. The package that the Americans then negotiated was a package that virtually anybody who had an interest in the United States was given an opportunity for input. That is not so in Canada. It is always secret. It is always left up to the Cabinet or the Department involved.
Customs Tariff
My suggestion to the Hon. Member would be that he make a case of what is happening in Lindsay and point out the repercussions that an import will have on employment in Canada. It is safe to say that every time we allow greater importation of goods, it is generally labour-intensive. What we are gaining on the other side through the exportation of goods is very low as far as labour is concerned. In short, we are exporting not only raw materials; in many cases we are exporting jobs with them. The manufacturing occurs in some other country, such as South Korea or Taiwan, and we import back. This cannot carry on. There is no way that we can solve the unemployment problem in this country-the projections made by the Minister of Finance confirm this-if we do not get a balanced trade position, especially on manufactured goods that are now S20 billion in deficit as far as overall trade is concerned.
I thank the Hon. Member for his question because it is really at the heart of why we should be getting more into this type of legislation than the Minister indicated when he said: "Let us give it speedy passage". Speedy passage has resulted in almost two million Canadians being out of work.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Debate. The Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour).

Mr. Speaker, in making a contribution to this debate, I would like to salute the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. MacLaren) for being present today. I would like to compliment him on the courage and candour of his remarks which were made yesterday on another trade matter at a conference held at the Lester B. Pearson Building. I might say that had he stayed yesterday for the rest of the speakers, he would have found their comments as equally interesting as his own, and perhaps, in some cases, more so. I do not mean to belittle his comments. There were a lot of interesting things said yesterday on the matter of proposed sectoral free trade between Canada and the United States.
