I would like to ask the Minister before he leaves why it is that a Bill such as the one we are discussing, Bill C-7, purports to help the Third World in a way that my colleagues have spoken about earlier, when at the same time as a Bill such as this is coming forward, members of the Opposition have representatives of governments coming to them asking why the Government of Canada is doing serious things in terms of their own economies. I am thinking, for example, of a person from Mauritius who came to see me not very long ago to ask why it was that the Government of Canada had unilaterally imposed a quota on cardigan sweaters from Mauritius which was threatening to throw their economy into considerable difficulty.
Mauritius is not a member of the fabric union. They have been debating with the Government of Canada for a long time about the state of the sweaters coming into Canada. They are good sweaters. It is an under-developed country. Suddenly, someone-I do not know whether it was the Minister himself-informed them that they would have a quota imposed on

May 2, 1984
Customs Tariff
them. Mauritius, I gather, is just getting on its feet economically. They are building up their manufacturing sector. It is a strategically important country to the West, situate as it is in the Indian Ocean. As a result, Mauritius has been hit very severely by a unilateral act by the Government of Canada with respect to one of its exports to Canada.
It is a member of the Commonwealth.

As the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) points out, it is a member of the Commonwealth.
Is it another example of the Government appearing to do something to help the Third World-we on this side are all for that, particularly with respect to trade-but on the other hand, behind the curtain, under the table, slipping a notice, in this case to Mauritius, telling them that they must not get uppity and put their people to work because they cannot export to Canada more than a given quantity of a particular item.
Mr. Speaker, if you have not had the pleasure of reading this Bill, please do not. It is enough to give anybody a headache. Even those of us who have spent much of our lives trying to interpret statutes in front of judges find it virtually incomprehensible-from the first clause, as the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) noted, to the last explanatory notes which are, shall we say, unhelpful. They provide no more light on the matter than the clauses themselves. I wonder why the Minister of State for Finance could not have produced something that was at least comprehensible to Canadians as a whole.
I am led to believe that the substance of the Bill is as follows. It will provide for tariff reductions for goods from developing countries-that is the general preferential tariff- and tariff reductions will be provided for various goods not produced in Canada, such as diesel engines for crawler machines and electronic carillons for churches. There will be increases for certain "wear" parts of machinery. These changes were announced in the Budget of April 19. The tariff reductions are retroactive to October 20, 1983. The tariff increases will not take effect until proclaimed. The date of the proclamation for increases will not be determined until the conclusion of the ongoing GATT negotiations.
Second, the limits on goods that may be brought back into Canada by Canadians travelling abroad are doubled. What person of good will and reason would object to that? Certainly, Mr. Speaker, your wife and mine and the wives of anyone who is able to travel abroad would support that.
The quarterly exemption is increased to $100 from $50. The annual exemption rises to $300 from $150, and the casual exemption rises to $20 from $10. These measures are retroactive to April 20, 1983.
Third, the Bill points out that the expiry date for the general preferential tariff has been moved to June 30, 1994 from June 30, 1984.
Parts of the Bill, Mr. Speaker, are almost funny. They are housekeeping measures. As other speakers might have pointed
out earlier, certain mynah birds, which have traditionally been allowed into the country, are members of the starling family which are not allowed into the country. The Act has been amended to exempt the Chinese Talking Mynah and the Hill Mynah.
Fourth, in the humour section-and that is not humour at all-the wording of some of the clauses of the French version are revised. There is some clarification that goods eligible for the general preferential tariff may be produced in more than one eligible country.
Finally, the Bill provides Order in Council authority to exempt goods from the need to be shipped directly from the country of origin to qualify for the general preferential tariff.
There are approximately 3,500 customs officials across Canada. Very recently, one of the customs officials came to speak with me. He indicated that customs officers are given no training whatsoever. They are essentially presented with the leaflets that Canadian tourists and Canadian travellers are given and in effect, I gather, are told to enforce the law. How can any competent customs officer interpret the provisions of amendments such as these? The Hon. Member for York-Peel referred-he may not have used the term Byzantine-to the eleven amendments which have been made to the Customs Tariff in the past number of years.
Unless we train our customs officials, I am told it is simply impossible for them to administer the laws passed by this Parliament. If it is impossible to enforce and interpret provisions of a Bill such as this, what is the point, I ask you, Mr. Speaker, of all of us sitting here at so much an hour passing Bills like this which are going to be unenforceable and incomprehensible to the men and women who have to interpret the various provisions?
I end on that point with a plea to the Government at least to provide training to new customs officers and to provide adequate manuals. The Minister may argue that they have manuals, but again I have information from someone who works every day in the field that the manuals are so huge and so difficult to interpret that most customs officers do not even bother to refer to them, at least in some areas. I would assume that would include the area we are talking about today.
On the question of the developing world, if I may, I would like to associate myself with what has been said by others, particularly my colleague, the Hon. Member for Edmonton South (Mr. Roche). He has been interested in the Third World for virtually a lifetime and what he says, Mr. Speaker, I feel should carry immense weight in this House.
The Third World desperately needs to trade with the developed world. I have been told, as I am sure you have, Mr. Speaker, time and time again, that it does not want aid as much as it wants the ability to trade, and it cannot trade with us unless it has the right to have its goods enter Canada. To that extent I certainly support the spirit of the Bill, which is to provide for a tariff reduction for goods supplied by developing countries. Please let there be no doubt about that.
May 2, 1984

It is so hard to get to the more basic problems. Not very many years ago, Mr. Speaker, it was my good fortune to attend a conference on crime prevention in Venezuela. There were people there from all over the world, including the developing world. You appreciate, Mr. Speaker, we were talking about crime, and one of the representatives of, I believe, the Republic of India-stood up and told us that in his view the real crime was the fact that the developed world-the 15 or 20 countries which are considered to be developed- would go into world markets for oil, would buy spot oil at prices which certainly the Third World could not afford. In other words, as a result of Canada buying oil and bidding up the price of oil in the world spot markets, we were making it more and more difficult for Third World countries to buy the oil which they desperately needed to develop their own economies.
I wonder, Mr. Speaker, how many people who might hear my voice are, like myself, shamefully guilty of wasting energy from the time we get up in the morning to the time we go to bed at night? The wastage of energy in Canada is simply, in my view, obscene. We waste energy here in this building, with respect, Mr. Speaker. We waste it in our offices. Virtually since birth, most of us have acquired the habit of wasting energy at each and every conceivable opportunity. When we can turn on one light or ten lights, we do it. I was just looking at the lights in the ceiling of this Chamber and wondering why they are really necessary. I do not know how much it is costing an hour, but every one of those lights is on. I am sure the Chamber could operate as efficiently with less energy used.
It seems to me that before we can begin to help the Third World, we must look at some of its more basic problems. There is the question of Third World debt. Is it really useful for a country like Brazil or Mexico to be encouraged by the financial institutions, public and private, to bid up their debts to the maximum feasible extent, as they did during the last six or seven years, to be now in a position where in many cases their entire export earnings cannot pay the interest on their foreign debts? It seems to me, with respect, that is not a very good thing to encourage the Third World to do to itself.
I am told, Mr. Speaker, rightly or wrongly, that there are Canadians who had their loans called, or their credit cut back, because of the present need of the Canadian banking system to cover the indebtedness to it of the Third World. In effect, it seems to me Third World countries are being put into terribly difficult economic positions partly because of loans made by the Canadian banking system and partly because of conditions which have gone sour in many of those countries. And Canadians are losing their jobs, losing their businesses, in some cases losing their homes-and I speak of my own riding in that regard-by reason of loans being called and interest rates in the Canadian banking system going up.
May I be permitted, in passing, to point out that in Edmonton today we have, I am told, about 40 per cent unemployment in the construction industry. One of our malls put an advertisement in the paper for 200 summer jobs and 5,000 people showed up for those jobs, and they were summer jobs at that.
Customs Tariff
Another story out of Edmonton yesterday suggests that university students lined up-slept through the night in some cases- for the few jobs available through the Hire-a-Student Program.
I come back to the fact, Mr. Speaker, that over the last five years the so-called developed world has done a great deal to hurt the undeveloped, less developed or the developing economies of the world. I would like to make some points in this regard by quoting from a very penetrating article written not too long ago by Ivan Illich entitled "Outwitting the 'Developed' Countries". He points out that by persuading or pushing on to the developing world modern solutions we have caused them all sorts of grief. He said, and I quote from the article:
Rich nations now benevolently impose a straight jacket of traffic jams, hospital confinements, and classrooms on the poor nations, and by international agreement call this "development".... traffic jams develop in Sao Paolo, while almost a million northeastern Brazilians flee the drought by walking 500 miles. Latin American doctors get training at the New York Hospital for Special Surgery, which they apply to only a few, while amoebic dysentry remains endemic in slums where 90 per cent of the population live.
Buses are alternatives to a multitude of private cars. Vehicles designed for slow transportation on rough terrain are alternatives to standard trucks. Safe water is an alternative to high-priced surgery. Medical workers are an alternative to doctors and nurses. Community food storage is an alternative to expensive kitchen equipment. Other alternatives could be discussed by the dozen.
Why not, instead, make one or two months (of education) a year obligatory for all citizens (of Latin America) below the age of thirty? Money is now spent largely on children, but an adult can be taught to read in one tenth the time and for one tenth the cost it takes to teach a child ... not only can he (an adult) contribute to the education of his children, but to that of other adults as well.
Who here can disagree with the point which Mr. Illich, who is, I believe, a priest or a former priest, is making? The developed world, it seems to me, comes along with a Bill like this and says: "Look, developing world-we are so good to you we are going to extend the general preferential tariff on some of the items".
Let me list some of them. Just leafing through the Bill, Mr. Speaker, we are going to give them help on things like biscuits, not sweetened; biscuits, sweetened; orchids, sardines, shellfish, lobsters, caviar-I wonder about that. Then there is tobacco leaf, whisky, gin, rum, brandy, vodka and alcoholic perfumes, whatever they are. Do you drink them or put them on your arm? Vinegar, labels for cigar boxes, photographs, plans and drawings, music for mechanical piano players, matches of paper, shoe blacking, baths, toilet bowls, grindstones, logging cars, flooring tiles and woven fabrics, among others. We say we are going to continue a tariff preference on these items, but, by George, in the case of Canada's proposed trade aid fund we are going to make it absolutely certain that 80 per cent of what you need in your economy is going to come from Canadian producers, whether we have producers or not, it seems to me, in that particular field.
Essentially, Mr. Speaker, there is too much hypocrisy exhibited in Bills like this. I think it would be very helpful if all Members, especially a new government, were to look at some of the basic issues and deal with them rather than apply band-aids such as the one I am holding.

May 2, 1984
Customs Tariff

Mr. Speaker, perhaps the Hon. Member will know that the general preferential tariff, which is essentially for under-developed or less developed nations, still applies to countries like Brazil and South Korea. Both of those countries have been exporting fairly technical manufactured goods to the rest of the world and both restrict Canadian imports. Both countries have used the general preferential tariff to enter the Canadian market in a predatory fashion.
Is it the view of the Hon. Member that they should continue to receive this foreign aid, so to speak? Or should they have applied to them the ordinary tariffs, the same as any other manufacturing country? Is it his view that the general preferential tariff should be extended so as to cover virtually every fly-speck on the map in the sense that a country which really needs help does not get any more help than we give the south Koreas or Brazils of the world?

Mr. Speaker, I am very hesitant to try to compare tariff knowledge with the Hon. Member from Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). He is an expert on tariff matters. However, it seems to me that Brazil is still an undeveloped country that needs some help. Perhaps in his next question he could tell me what its average per capita income is. Obviously some people in Sao Paulo may be doing well but there are millions of Brazilians living outside of the major centres. If you could locate a plant in those areas, it seems to me they should then be entitled to export to Canada on a preferential tariff basis.
The Andean pact, which applies to Venezuela, for example, is proposing to reduce imports from countries like Canada over the next few years. Therefore, I wonder why Canada continues to buy about $1 billion worth of oil from Venezuela. I guess that has gone down in the last couple of years, but at the same time Venezuela is making it harder and harder through its membership in the Andean pact for Canadian oil processing and technical equipment to enter Venezuela. There is a whole range of goods, particularly in Alberta, that we would like to export to Venezuela but we are faced with the Andean pact tariff barrier. I guess that speaks to this question even if it does not answer it.

Mr. Speaker, there is no question that the standard of living and the general wealth of the average person in Brazil is not that great. However, the Hon. Member will know from being in Brazil that a great deal of the population lives in more than ordinary affluence. Some industries, particularly the aircraft industry, are operated in such a fashion as to seriously impede through predatory pricing the sales of Canadian aircraft, particularly those of de Havilland.
Is it the view of the Hon. Member that we should continue to give countries like Brazil that advantage when they do not seem to concern themselves about predatory practices and taking advantage in the Canadian market? Should we perhaps not play a little tougher when we run into predatory practices of people masquerading as under-developed countries or less developed countries when the poverty in those countries is
largely because they refuse to allow equal opportunities to their own citizens?

Mr. Speaker, so the record is clear, I have never been to Brazil. There was a suggestion in my colleague's question that I have been and it should not be allowed to stand on the record. If the Hon. Member is prepared to send me there at his expense, I will be happy to go.
I thought with your foreign trade experience you would know about that.

The question of aircraft is a very interesting one because it is my understanding that this industry is the one example of a truly internationalized industry. The industry all over the world has decided that you can make the steering wheel in Brazil, the engine in Britain and the fuselage somewhere else. As I understand it, there are very limited tariffs applicable to aircraft parts around the world. There is also the argument that that is the way the auto industry may-I underline "may"-go in the future. If it does, then presumably an under-developed Third World country might be capable of making the seat covers for all the planes built in the world. South Korea might produce something else, and Brazil something else. Barbados, for example, may produce a third item. The question of the aircraft industry is a fascinating one and I hope the Hon. Member makes a speech so I can ask him about how he sees the future of the industry as perhaps applicable to other sectors as well.

speechtext: Order. In the opinion of the Chair, Hon. Members are straying somewhat from the general contents of the Bill. I invite them to stick with the subject matter.

The Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) talked earlier about some of the concerns he had about this particular Bill. Parliament, he said, may have a little trouble scrutinizing the direction in which the Government is going and the kind of things it is trying to accomplish. One of his suggestions was the concept of having a committee study this type of situation. Would the Hon. Member who just spoke have some thoughts about the kind of committee he would envisage? Mr. Speaker, the question, which was not discussed before, gives me a chance to point out that I would like to see the committee consist of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, because it may astound you, Mr. Speaker, to know that to the best of my knowledge that committee has not met formally on any matter other than estimates since June 9, 1983.
It is rather odd that members of all Parties want to get on that Committee yet the Committee, for all intents and purposes, never meets.

It does not do anything.
May 2, 1984

It does not do anything, as the Member for Edmonton South (Mr. Roche) says. As best as I can determine-I know that the Chairman of the Committee will be mad at me for this-the Chairman does not seem to be very interested in having it do anything and certainly the Minister is not interested in having it do anything.
Interested in cocktail parties.
The Minister or the Chairman?
The Chairman.

May it be very clear, Mr. Speaker, that that comment is coming from the Member for Edmonton South. It is a very important point that if there is to be a standing committee representing democracy in Canada in an important area like that, there are 100 things it should be doing, including the matter raised by the Member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper), rather than sitting, waiting and primarily having basically informal discussions with visiting people from around the world. While that may be interesting, there is much more the Committee should be doing, possibly including the matter referred to by the Member for Peace River.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Debate.

Mr. Speaker, we have had some fascinating debates with regard to customs over the years. I have been participating in customs tariff debates since 1963. It is always a challenge to ask the Minister or Parliamentary Secretary concerned with the legislation to refer to the various schedules and numbers and read out what is in the customs tariff. They supposedly know their way around. I must confess that few, if any, have ever been able to do so and even fewer have ever expressed a desire to do so.
In these various schedules there are all of these numbers, columns and various exceptions included in it and finally at the bottom there is always the phrase for all the category items "not otherwise provided for". It becomes rather confusing.
Clearly there are some interesting provisions here. One needs only to look at Clause 1(3) to see that the Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour) was right on with regard to the development of what could be called world industry. Even some of our Canadian firms, such as Massey-Ferguson, will put engines constructed in Italy by Fiat or by other firms from Scotland into their tractors or combines. Of course, automobiles are made from an amalgamation of goods from many places. Let us not forget about TV sets and video component assemblies. Some stage of their manufacture perhaps will take place in Taiwan and then come to the United States or even Canada, notwithstanding the purists in the Department of External Affairs, because Canada does have some commercial relations with Taiwan. There are other examples.
It is only fair that a finished article being imported into the country should have a level of duty for Canadian purposes determined by the value of the goods in the country in which
Customs Tariff
the components were made. Otherwise, the process becomes totally inaccurate.
Let me give an example of when I believe I beat the Department. I was sent some cigars from the Philippines in a very heavy wooden box. In fact, the box weighed far more than the cigars. The clerk placed this on the scale and wrote the figure based on the duty on tobacco. There was not only the tobacco duty but sales tax as well. The box itself was not taken into account. I had a final assessment of approximately $25, I believe, which I thought was rather excessive. I believe $17 was returned to me. I inquired about the box and the wrappings for which they were charging me. While I did not object to the assessment of the cigars, the carved wooden box was another matter. Frankly, at the time I received a wooden cigar box for free as far as duty was concerned. I did not say anything because it would have confused them. They would not have been able to figure it out, other than by charging me the total price for cigars.
I believe we should get more explanation from the Minister or the Parliamentary Secretary with respect to Clause 10 since it is retroactive to April 20, 1983. While undoubtedly there are very good reasons for putting this clause forward, it is incumbent upon the Minister to come forward and say precisely what this effect will have. Does it mean that duties which were formerly leviable against certain commodities are now being moved back and the retroactive date will be April 20? Certainly one would hope that there will not be the imposition of additional duties dating back from April 20, 1983, and that this Bill will be the authority for having levied those additional duties.
I think the House will agree completely that with respect to the special tariff that is levied under the general preferential tariff for Third World countries, one would like to see what effect it has had now that it has been in place for approximately ten years. While it is proposed to extend it for another ten years, has it really met the stated objectives at the time of its introduction? As I recall, it was introduced by the Finance Minister of the day, John Turner. He introduced that measure with a view to giving a particular break to Third World countries in so far as our tariff schedules were concerned. But has it worked? Has there been an improvement in trade from those countries to Canada? If not, it is useless.
I would hope that the Minister can come forward with some figures which will show that while not all Third World countries have benefited, a number of them have benefited from the lowering of duties under this particular preferential tariff.
There are always humorous things in the customs tariff. I came across some right in the very early pages. Let us look at page 4, Clause 8. It reads:
The French version of Schedule A to the said Act is further amended by adding immediately after the reference to "a ciel ouvert"-
In other words, "open sky", which is the term to be used. The clause continues:
-in tariff item 49217-1, a reference to-

May 2, 1984
Customs Tariff
The English would be "and their pieces". This is going to make a fascinating examination. I am sorry I have not had time to do so. But what on earth are they talking about in Clause 8 when they talk about "open sky"? Then we have this number 49217. I suppose one could have a quick look to see if 49217 is mentioned at all.
It isn't.

That is all right, then. It does not have to be. It can be in the tariff. I will have a look at my copy. But then Clause 9 reads:
Schedule C to the said Act is amended by repealing paragraph (2) of item 99214-1 -
And then we wonder. It continues in (2):
Any bird of the Starling family (Sturnidae) except the European Starling (Sturnus vulgaris)-
And then what is added? It continues:
-and the Chinese Talking Mynah or Hill Mynah (Gracula religiosa);
This is also fascinating insofar as these particular ones are concerned.
Then we can look over the various items under Schedule 1 which are being changed. We get the distinction between non-sweetened biscuits and sweetened biscuits, orchids, sardines, sprats or pilchards when they weigh so much. Then we have shellfish, lobster, and caviar. I want to draw this to the particular attention of the Chair because there is a very serious distinction between the Excise Act and the Excise Tax Act. Here on page 6 of Schedule 1 we find tobacco unmanufactured, for excise purposes under conditions of the Excise Act where there is a duty payable and not a tax.
Here we have "not otherwise provided for-unstemmed tobacco when imported by cigar manufacturers. Then we find stemmed when imported by cigar manufacturers for use in cigars. Then we find whiskey, gin and rum. All of these are being incidentally extended for the general preferential tariff. I suppose that means that certain ministers of the provinces will go running down to the Caribbean countries at the time of the CPA annual meetings and negotiate the best deal they can get for their various liquor commissions for liquors particularly exported from the Caribbean countries. There is a good deal, I must say, about liquor in this Bill, Mr. Speaker.
Then we move from liquor to vinegar. However, as I said, one could have a much more detailed examination of all these changes if one had the total schedule of the Customs Tariff before one. They have a very serious effect in various parts of the country. It is not known what the effect would be of really moving to free trade with either the world or the United States or to counter the Common Market.
I remember attending a conference some years ago in New York with regard to the establishment of a Japanese-North American trading bloc to counter the Common Market. There were a lot of fine theories put forward at that time, but we note that nothing has been done, and I have not heard anything more in at least 15 years about this type of, shall we
say, setting up a counter trading bloc with the European Common Market.
Our Customs Tariff has been the subject of some very severe criticisms in the past. In my experience here in this House we have gone through both the Kennedy round and the Tokyo round which, in effect, is something like 18 to 20 years of experience in dealing with the reclassifications under the Canadian Customs Tariff. I understand that there is another Bill as well having to do with the Anti-Dumping Tribunal. I think if my memory serves me correctly that Bill will do something with regard to classifications of items in order that there is a uniformity of definition or description and one does not discriminate against any particular country in invoking anti-dumping provisions.
With regard to our own Customs Tariff, we have seen a lot of reduction. The one thing I do not like is not so much what is in the Customs Tariff Act as content but behaviour under the Customs Act. We have had action taken by the administration at the present time with regard to textiles, finished textiles, high quality ones, where there were slowdowns at the ports of entry and now we are having some difficulty. I had a call from a number of importers or dealers in computer parts which had to be sent back to the United States where they are manufactured. They had to be sent back for repair and then re-entered.
Unfortunately there are times when the staffs at certain of the airports, the customs officers, are absolutely swamped. They get a sort of annual average establishment. Unfortunately there are periods when there is an awful lot of traffic. Notwithstanding the fact that certain limited local additions may be made, the customers are kept waiting. There was an occasion last week where if a representative of a firm had not gone out to the airport and pounded on the counter to get, shall we say, earlier service than that company would have had, and then taken the part the representative obtained and gone helter-skelter to Calgary by car, the company would have lost the account because competition is very tight. Unless people are able to deliver a service, the account is lost.
Sometimes this is not appreciated in the service departments of government like customs where, frankly, customers are told; "We have handled so much today that we are not handling any more". It was not closing time but they had been under the gun all day. Local superintendents have advised me that they are looking into this matter and will take the necessary action under the Customs Act. But we could take a long time to study the customs tariff. Many more Members of the House could take an interest in it in order to understand the effect of certain proposals. This is the one Bill which is the least understood of all legislation. It is fed down the pipe and people simply say: "Let it go on the nod". That should not be. Such is the nature of the Customs Tariff Bill that it is difficult to understand and few people pay attention to it, yet they are very seriously affected by it from time to time.
I hope the Bill will go through Committee of the Whole and ultimately receive passage. I understand that certain features
May 2, 1984

of it are needed and overdue in the Department of National Revenue on the customs side. However, the fault for that lies with the Government in waiting so long to bring forward the Bill for discussion in the House. Then the Minister arrives and says: "Rush, rush, rush; we need it". That is hypocrisy and bad management in the House.
I am taking my time to say these things because they have to be said. I refuse to be stampeded by being told that the Department needs this Bill now or needed it yesterday. It should have been brought forward a month ago.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Questions or comments? On debate, the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby).

Mr. Speaker, second reading of Bill C-7, an Act to amend the Customs Tariff, provides an opportunity to discuss two subjects of major importance to Canada. First and foremost, the Bill involves in an indirect way international trade and, second, it involves in a very direct way Revenue Canada, both in its administration and in relation to the laws it administers.
Let me begin by reviewing those two main features of Bill C-7. The Bill provides special tariff considerations for goods produced in so-called developing countries, otherwise known as the Third World. Of course, these are goods which are not available in Canada that we can allow to be imported without affecting similar goods processed within Canada. There is no exact similarity in the kinds of goods which will be permitted to be imported from Third World nations.
This legislative initiative through customs tariff arrangements allows us to consider the whole aspect of international trade, its effect on the Canadian economy and on Canadian people. Also we have to deal with Revenue Canada, both in its administration of the laws and with respect to the laws themselves. Bill C-7 changes the dollar values applicable to goods brought into Canada by residents of Canada who are returning from foreign travel. These changes in the dollar values of goods imported in this way are very substantially increased. As I understand it, for long term periods outside Canada, seven days or more, a Canadian resident can bring back $300 worth of goods. That is an increase of $150 over the previous dollar standards. The same applies in terms of the percentage increase for goods which can be returned to Canada after a shorter stay, that is, an increase of $50 to $100.
For some people who travel abroad and return to Canada with goods, this is a very substantial increase. I know from personal experience that some Canadian residents in their foreign travel would take that as immediate legislative authority to double the amount of goods they bring into Canada on their return. In some cases that is very substantial. I know people who upon returning from shopping trips in the United States bring back a large amount of goods and claim a value of $150. In some cases they require a truck when they return because they take that legislative, mandated increase as au-
Customs Tariff
thority to double their purchases and in that way increase the amounts of goods and services they bring back to Canada.
I have never known Canadians to overestimate the value of goods which they brought back to Canada. That is to say, I have never known them to say that the goods they brought back were substantially more in terms of dollar value than the restrictions allowed. I say that only partly with tongue in cheek because I do not know how Revenue Canada would ever be able to ascertain the total dollar amounts involved in a change such as this.
I want to speak about this more directly with respect to the administration of the revenue laws by Revenue Canada, because it is in an area where a great deal of judgment must be exercised by the administrators of the law. I do not suppose there is a customs officer on any border point in Canada who does not see time and time again Canadians returning with goods which they must suspect are greatly in excess of the dollar values permitted. However, what action should they take? Should they bother in every case that they encounter to demand proof of the value of the goods or otherwise attempt to assess the value by some objective standard?
The point I want to make and underline is: Is this another case in which the government through the legislative process will create a situation that will result in difficulties for Canadian citizens? In other words, is the Government inviting Canadians to bring back more and more goods from foreign travel and then find when they arrive at the border point that they have to submit themselves to a rigorous examination process which will possibly result in violations of laws of Canada, in prosecutions, in other enforcement actions or in imposition of sanctions in respect of those laws?
To put it bluntly, is this a case in which Canadian citizens will be lulled into thinking that the Government of Canada does not really care that much about the dollar value of the goods they bring back to Canada and, having given Canadians that impression, it then imposes with great force the full burden of the law? I would like to know the answer to that question. I hope in any final disposition of the Bill that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) will make very clear the exact instructions which will be issued to customs officers with respect to the enforcement of these new dollar values.
I should explain quickly that Revenue Canada, as it is commonly known, is actually the Department of National Revenue with two specific divisions, as I understand it-first, Customs and Excise and, second, Taxation. We in the House of Commons know all about the activities of Revenue Canada in its Taxation division. We know all about the harsh administration of tax laws. We know all about the quota systems imposed by senior officers in Revenue Canada, Taxation. But we know very little about Revenue Canada on the customs and excise side. I can state from my experience that customs officers can be equally difficult and present similar difficulties to Canadian residents as the officers of Revenue Canada, Taxation.

May 2, 1984
Customs Tariff
I do not underestimate the importance of the duties performed by the officers of Revenue Canada, either on the customs and excise side or on the taxation side. The statistics I have from the Department of National Revenue report from 1983 indicate that the Taxation division of Revenue Canada produced revenues of $56.9 billion, a very substantial portion of the total revenue of Canada. As I understand the statistics, the customs and excise side produced $3.2 billion in revenue. That is revenue from a variety of taxes including import duties, sales tax, excise tax and other excise taxes and duties. 1 suppose added to that are what are called sundry collections. That division of the Department of National Revenue, that is, Customs and Excise, has a wide variety of laws to administer.
As Members of Parliament and representatives of the people, our duty is to ensure two things: first, that the laws enacted by Parliament are fair in their application to the people subject to them; second, that the public administration of the laws, in this case by the Customs and Excise division of Revenue Canada, is fair. One is justified in addressing both of those points in the context of Bill C-7 because we now have reason to believe, as a result of our experience with Revenue Canada on the taxation side, that the administration of the laws may be questionable.
Those are the two points 1 want to make with respect to the provisions of Bill C-7 that relate to the importation of goods by Canadian travellers, namely that the written law be clear and that the administration of the law be fair to Canadians.
That brings me to this point. What we have done in Bill C-7 is double the value of goods that can be brought into Canada by travellers from abroad, as I have said several times. However, all of us in this Chamber know that Canadians are in the habit of giving a liberal interpretation to that designation of dollar value. Without naming names, I suspect there are many Canadians who bring back literally hundreds of dollars worth of goods into Canada, the value of which cannot be easily determined. I suspect in the normal course of things that some Canadians will interpret this change in the law as a permit to double the amount of goods they bring back.
I would like to know from the Minister of National Revenue how the officers will interpret these new dollar limitations. Will this be enforced more strictly than in the past or will they recognize that what the Parliament of Canada has authorized in Bill C-7 is an increase of 100 per cent of what has gone on in the past? In other words, Canadians who brought in a certain amount of goods and material on return to Canada may now feel free to double the quantity of goods and materials they are in the habit of bringing back to Canada. Will they now be faced with strict enforcement and will that result in the imposition of sanctions and penalties which are included in the law?
The reason I am so concerned about that is that there seems to be a tendency among law enforcers, whether they are involved in revenue or penal laws, including criminal laws, to demand stricter enforcement. Stricter enforcement of the law seems to be the order of the day. I want to say something very generally about strict enforcement of the laws. I am appalled by the situation that we often find ourselves in where relatively innocent citizens, those who contribute to the economy, work on a day-to-day basis, and so on, are called to task for minor infractions such as failing to file an income tax return on time or some other minor infraction of income tax law, some minor infraction of the traffic laws or laws that relate to hunting regulations and that sort of thing. More citizens are brought before the courts of Canada for those kinds of infractions than on serious criminal charges.
If we want to stamp out illegal activity in Canada and want to use the resources of government to do that, let us stamp out rape, murder, robbery and housebreaks. Never mind stamping out the minor infractions of Canadian citizens which they commit inadvertently or without any guilty intent, such as exceeding the values that relate to goods they bring into Canada on return from travel abroad.
I am told there are certain advantages to increasing the amounts that apply to goods brought into Canada by Canadians returning from foreign travel. Certainly the inflation we have experienced in the past decade justifies a substantial increase in its own right. It is my sincere hope that this will not result in a substantial change in the manner in which these laws are enforced, or it will end up to the detriment of those we are trying to benefit, our fellow Canadians.
We have reason not to trust the administration of Revenue Canada with respect to this kind of change in the law. Let me say very quickly that I have great confidence in the public servants of Canada, particularly those in the service of the Department of National Revenue. However, like any employees, they require clear direction. Employees require a code and management direction that makes it very clear what their responsibilities are and how they are to administer the laws which they are charged with.
I want to take this opportunity to say to the Minister of National Revenue and those who serve directly under him that they should make certain in the administration of this new law that instructions are given that will be consistent with the intent of this law, which is to benefit Canadians returning from foreign travel. Keep that in mind and make it the guide. This is a law to benefit Canadians, not a law to change the administration of our revenue laws.
I mentioned international trade. As I said, that subject is implicit in the provisions of Bill C-7 that relate to importation of goods from the Third World.
May 2, 1984

I see the clock is approaching six. I will take the remaining minute to underline the importance of international trade to Canada. We have had a dramatic increase in our trading capacity over the past decade. I understand that at present our international trade amounts to approximately 30 per cent of our Gross National Product. The 1982 figure for our international trade is $84.6 billion. It becomes immediately evident that that is a very substantial sum of money when you consider
Customs Tariff
that the total amount spent by Canada as a nation on government business is $100 billion. I see the clock is approaching six.
